note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Young female with 2-day history of gradually worsening, constant burning suprapubic (just below the umbilicus) abdominal pain with mild nausea, subjective feverishness/sweats, new urinary frequency and reported pink-coloured urine; clinician empirically treated for suspected lower urinary tract infection and recommended pregnancy testing and follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Lower central abdominal (suprapubic) pain for ~2 days; described as burning and sore to pressure.
  - Associated subjective feverishness/hot sweats, mild nausea, increased urinary frequency, and noticed pink-coloured urine.
- Timeline / progression:
  - Symptoms began ~2 days ago, gradual onset, described as fairly constant and worsening.
  - Prior constipation last week that has since improved; current bowel movements reported as normal.
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - Pain is worse with pressure on the area (patient reports it is "sore when I press on it").
  - No specific relieving factors reported; patient remains ambulatory and functioning.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems (as reported):
  - GU: Increased urinary frequency; pink-coloured urine; denies dysuria or burning on urination.
  - GI: Mild nausea; no vomiting.
  - Constitutional: Feels hot and sweaty (no measured temperature recorded).
  - Respiratory / Cardiac / Neuro / Vision: Denies shortness of breath, cough, palpitations, headaches, visual changes.
  - Gynecologic: Sexually active with one partner; Implanon implant placed ~1 year ago; last sexual activity ~4 days ago; last period approximately 2 weeks ago; last STI screen normal ~6 months ago.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No vomiting, no objective fever recorded, no dysuria, no abnormal vaginal discharge reported, no flank pain or radiating pain to groin described.

Past Medical History:
- Medical conditions:
  - Reports generally fit and well; no chronic medical conditions documented.
- Surgical history:
  - No prior surgeries.
- Medications:
  - Contraception: Implanon implant (inserted ~1 year ago).
  - No other regular medications documented.
- Allergies:
  - Not documented.

Social History:
- Living situation: Lives in a share house with two roommates.
- Occupation: Accountant.
- Tobacco: Denies smoking.
- Alcohol: Social drinking; no excess use documented.
- Illicit substances: Not mentioned.

Family History:
- No relevant family history reported or known by patient.

Physical Examination:
- Vital signs:
  - No vitals recorded in the transcript.
- Examination findings:
  - Patient reports suprapubic tenderness when pressing on the area ("quite sore when I press on it"). (No formal clinician exam findings documented.)

Investigations:
- None completed or resulted at time of consult.
- Tests discussed / recommended by clinician:
  - Urine testing (urinalysis/urine testing) to evaluate for UTI / hematuria — clinician stated tests could be arranged.
  - Pregnancy test recommended (patient asked to consider or perform pregnancy test).
  - No imaging or blood tests ordered during the visit in the transcript.

Assessment & Plan:
- Integration of transcript and DDx: Clinical picture most consistent with an acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) given suprapubic burning pain, urinary frequency and discoloured urine; other considerations include urolithiasis and gynecologic causes (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian pathology), which remain in the differential and warrant targeted testing and follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen.

- Issue 1: Suspected acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis)
  - Assessment:
    - High clinical suspicion based on suprapubic burning pain/tenderness, increased urinary frequency, and pink-coloured urine; mild systemic symptoms (nausea, subjective sweats).
  - Plan (supported by transcript):
    - Empiric antibiotic prescribed: Trimethoprim (as documented in consultation). Prescription instructions stated in the encounter as "you can take two tablets, uh, one tablet twice a day for three days." (Ambiguity/conflict noted—see Quality checks.)
    - Arrange / perform urine testing (urinalysis ± urine microscopy and culture) to confirm infection and assess for hematuria.
    - Symptomatic care: Paracetamol for pain/fever; maintain adequate oral fluids; cranberry juice suggested by clinician.
    - Safety-net / follow-up: Return or contact clinic if symptoms do not improve within a few days, or sooner if worsening abdominal pain, persistent or worsening fever/sweats, vomiting, or other concerning signs.

- Issue 2: Possible urolithiasis / urinary tract bleeding (hematuria)
  - Assessment:
    - Moderate likelihood per DDx: pink-coloured urine could represent hematuria from stone; lower abdominal pain and nausea can occur with distal urinary stones.
  - Plan (supported by transcript/DDx reasoning):
    - Evaluate urine testing results for microscopic/macroscopic hematuria.
    - If hematuria persists or pain becomes more severe/colicky or radiates to flank/groin, consider imaging (e.g., non-contrast CT KUB or ultrasound) and urology review — to be arranged based on test results or clinical deterioration.
    - Continue symptomatic management and reassess.

- Issue 3: Gynecologic causes including pregnancy-related complications or ovarian pathology
  - Assessment:
    - Moderate likelihood per DDx: ectopic pregnancy or ovarian cyst/ torsion can present with lower abdominal pain and bleeding; Implanon reduces but does not eliminate pregnancy risk.
  - Plan (supported by transcript):
    - Recommend pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy/ectopic pregnancy (patient advised to take a test; clinician discussed arranging testing).
    - If pregnancy test positive or if pain worsens or becomes unilateral/severe, arrange urgent gynecologic/obstetric assessment and relevant imaging (pelvic ultrasound) per clinical indications.
    - Consider STI testing / pelvic exam if clinical picture suggests PID (not currently indicated given history and exam).

- Additional / general plan items from transcript:
  - Patient education: advised to take paracetamol as needed, stay well hydrated, and return earlier if symptoms worsen (worsening pain, high fever, vomiting).
  - Prescription: script to be sent to patient’s pharmacy per clinician; patient instructed to start antibiotics today.
  - Follow-up: clinician requested patient re-presents if no improvement in a few days or sooner if deterioration.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- 1) Acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis)
  - Likelihood: High
  - Rationale: Burning suprapubic pain, urinary frequency, and pink-coloured urine consistent with lower UTI; clinician empirically treated for UTI.
- 2) Urolithiasis (ureteric/bladder stone)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Hematuria (pink urine) and lower abdominal pain with nausea can indicate distal stone; less typical features present (no severe colicky/flank-to-groin radiation documented).
- 3) Gynecologic cause — ectopic pregnancy or ovarian pathology (ruptured cyst/ovarian torsion)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Lower central pelvic pain and possible bleeding could reflect gynecologic causes; patient has Implanon (lowers pregnancy risk) and reports recent normal STI screen, but pregnancy/gynecologic pathology cannot be excluded without testing.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate) not recorded.
  - Allergies not documented.
  - Complete medication reconciliation not documented (only Implanon mentioned).
  - Formal clinician-performed abdominal / pelvic examination findings not documented (only patient-reported tenderness to self-pressing).
  - Results of urine testing and pregnancy test not available.
- Conflicts or ambiguities:
  - Medication instruction ambiguity: clinician said both "two tablets" and "one tablet twice a day for three days" regarding Trimethoprim during the encounter—conflict/ambiguity noted regarding exact dose; prescription should be confirmed with prescribing clinician/pharmacy.
  - No direct conflicts between transcript and DDx content; DDx expands potential causes consistent with the clinical story.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Transcript contains some hesitations/disfluencies but the clinical history and plan are clearly documented and interpretable.
